resources.string: Sends this phone\'s location to your family
Shows while tracker is sharing this phone\'s location with your family.
tracker is reporting this phone\'s position to your family server.
Collection can run in the background
tracker needs location access to report where this phone is. The next screen is the system permission prompt.
To keep reporting when the app is closed, tracker needs background location. This is a second, separate prompt — Android will not ask for both at once.
On Android 11 and later the permission prompt has no “Allow all the time” option — it can only be set in system settings. Open settings, choose Permissions → Location, and pick “Allow all the time”.
Android will no longer show the permission prompt for this app. Open settings and grant location access there.
tracker can collect location continuously, including while the app is closed.
Background location is not granted. Collection works while the app is open, but Android will stop it once the app is closed — the trail will have gaps.
Only approximate location is granted, so positions may be off by a city block. Grant precise location for an accurate trail.
Notifications are blocked, so the ongoing “sharing your location” notice will not be visible. Collection still runs.

The device token is stored unencrypted in this app\'s private data on the phone until secure storage ships (roadmap C3). On a non-rooted phone with a lock screen no other app can read it, but anyone with root, an unlocked bootloader or a full-device backup can. Cloud backup of the app\'s data is already switched off.

Save reports the verdict of validating what you typed, never a blanket “Saved”. A URL the app will refuse to use says so on the card in a few words, and the full sentence naming what to fix is shown at the top of this page. A release build also refuses plain http, so a shipped app cannot send a bearer credential in the clear.

Fixes are saved on this phone until the server confirms them, so going offline delays reporting instead of losing it. “dropped” means a fix the server permanently refused, one older than 90 days, or one discarded because the offline queue filled up.

Delivered counts fixes the server accepted during THIS run of the app, from the moment collection started. It is not a lifetime total and it is not restored from disk: after a restart the honest answer is “not recorded”, not a stale number. It counts an idempotent replay the server already had as delivered, so it can over-count a fix that was sent twice.

Queued counts fixes currently sitting in the on-disk queue, read from the queue itself rather than counted in memory — which is why it survives a restart when the other two do not. A non-zero value is normal, not an error: it is what the queue looks like while the phone is offline, and it is the number that says nothing has been lost.

Dropped counts fixes measured during this run that will never reach the server. It is shown as prominently as Delivered on purpose: an app that only ever displays its successes is how silent fix loss stays silent.

A counter that has never been measured reads “not recorded”, never 0 and never a dash. A measured zero still reads 0, because “we checked and it is none” and “we never checked” are different facts and a reader deciding whether their family\'s trail has a hole in it needs to be able to tell them apart. If the queue directory cannot be read at all, the queued figure alone reads “unavailable” and everything else on the screen keeps working.

When something stops collection or delivery, the card names the KIND of trouble in a few words - server settings incomplete, location permission lost, Android refused collection, reporting failed, device token rejected - and the sentence describing exactly what happened is shown at the top of this page. The sentence is kept off the card because it is not ours to keep short: a network failure or an Android exception supplies its own wording, and a paragraph on a phone card is a paragraph nobody reads.

Alerts are still being checked. This phone asks the server whether it is registered and which push backend the server uses, and that answer has not come back yet. The crossings list below does not wait for it.

No viewer token has been entered yet, so this phone is not registered and no crossings can be read. Run \"tracker add-viewer\" on the server and paste the token into the Server card above. Until then an empty list is not an empty family log, it is an app that has not been given a credential.

Notifications are blocked for this app, so a crossing cannot be shown as one however well the rest of the path works. Grant the notification permission in system settings. Crossings are still read and still listed below while it is blocked.
The server refused this viewer token, so this phone is not registered to receive alerts. Check the token in the Server card above; a device token is refused on this route by construction.
This phone could not reach the server to register for alerts. Check the server address in the Server card above, then reopen the app to try again.

This phone has no usable push configuration, so there is no address to register. An app built with no Firebase project in it reaches this state, and so does a phone whose push service is unavailable. Crossings are still listed below.

This server has no push backend configured, so it will never send an alert whatever this phone does. The registration is stored anyway, so configuring a backend later starts alerts without registering again. Crossings are still listed below.
This server sends through a push backend this app cannot receive from. This app receives from Firebase Cloud Messaging only. Crossings are still listed below.
This server does not report which push backend it uses, so this app cannot tell whether one is configured at all. It is older than the field that reports it. Crossings are still listed below.

A viewer token is entered, this phone is registered with the backend the server says it uses, and notifications are permitted, so a crossing will arrive as a notification. Arrival is still never guaranteed, which is why the list below is the record and the notification is not.

The crossings list states which of four things happened, and they are deliberately different sentences. \"No crossings recorded yet\" means the server was asked and answered with nothing. Each \"Crossings unread\" state means the list could NOT be read - a rejected token, a server that could not be reached, or an answer this app could not parse - and none of those is an empty family log.

A push that does not carry a complete crossing - its kind, the device name, the Place name and the direction - renders no notification, and is counted here instead. No missing part of it is guessed at, and the count is shown rather than kept quiet, because a discarded push is an alert somebody did not get.
The push backend holds only four pending alerts per phone, one per device-and-place pair, and then discards the rest. This list, read back from your server, is the record; the notification is not.

The viewer token is stored unencrypted in this app\'s private data, exactly as the device token is, until secure storage ships (roadmap SECRET-3). It reads the whole family\'s crossings, so treat it as the more sensitive of the two. Cloud backup of the app\'s data is already switched off.

While collection is running and a fix has arrived within the reporting interval, the counters are labelled as current. When collection is stopped, has been killed by the system, or has produced no fix for longer than that interval, the same counters are labelled “last known” with the time they were last updated. A frozen readout is never presented as a live one, and when collection resumes the counters go back to reading as current.
Tells you when a family member arrives at or leaves a place you have defined.
